questions.question: What is a key-value store?

options.text: A simple database that stores data as key-value pairs, like a hash map

questions.explanation: Key-value stores: simplest NoSQL model. Store and retrieve values by unique keys. Like a distributed hash table. Examples: Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB, etcd. Extremely fast for simple lookups.

questions.question: What operations do key-value stores typically support?

options.text: GET, PUT, DELETE—basic CRUD by key

questions.explanation: Core operations: GET(key), PUT(key, value), DELETE(key). Some support: TTL, atomic increments, conditional writes. No joins, limited querying. Simplicity enables extreme performance.

questions.question: When would you choose a key-value store?

options.text: Caching, session storage, real-time data where access is by known keys

questions.explanation: Key-value stores excel at: caching (Redis/Memcached), session storage, user preferences, shopping carts, real-time leaderboards. When you know the key and need fast access. Not for complex queries.

questions.question: What is the difference between Redis and Memcached?

options.text: Redis: data structures, persistence, replication; Memcached: simpler, multi-threaded, pure cache

questions.explanation: Redis: rich data types (lists, sets, hashes), persistence options, replication, Lua scripting. Memcached: simpler, multi-threaded (better for simple caching at scale), no persistence. Choose based on needs.

questions.question: What data structures does Redis support beyond simple strings?

options.text: Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, Hashes, Streams, HyperLogLog

questions.explanation: Redis data structures: Strings, Lists (queues), Sets (unique items), Sorted Sets (leaderboards), Hashes (objects), Streams (event logs), HyperLogLog (cardinality), Bitmaps. Very versatile.

questions.question: How do key-value stores achieve high performance?

options.text: Simple data model, in-memory storage, O(1) hash-based lookups

questions.explanation: Performance from: hash-based O(1) lookups, in-memory storage (Redis, Memcached), simple data model (no joins/parsing), minimal overhead. Sub-millisecond latency for most operations.

questions.question: What is a limitation of key-value stores?

options.text: No querying by value—you must know the key; no relationships or complex queries

questions.explanation: Limitations: must know key to retrieve (no 'find all users where age > 30'), no joins, no secondary indexes (usually), limited transaction support. Design keys carefully for your access patterns.

questions.question: What is etcd used for?

options.text: Distributed configuration and service discovery (used by Kubernetes)

questions.explanation: etcd: distributed key-value store for configuration, service discovery, leader election. Uses Raft for consensus. Kubernetes stores all cluster state in etcd. Strong consistency, not for high-throughput caching.

questions.question: How does DynamoDB differ from Redis as a key-value store?

options.text: DynamoDB: managed, persistent, scalable, supports secondary indexes; Redis: in-memory, faster, richer data types

questions.explanation: DynamoDB: fully managed, auto-scaling, persistent, global tables, secondary indexes. Redis: in-memory (faster), rich data structures, pub/sub. DynamoDB for durable storage, Redis for caching/real-time.

questions.question: What is key design important in key-value stores?

options.text: Keys determine access patterns—must encode all query dimensions into the key
Keys should be as long as possible

questions.explanation: Key design is crucial: user:123:profile, order:456:items. Encode entity type, ID, and attribute. Can't query by value, so key must contain everything needed to locate data. Composite keys for range queries.

questions.question: What is TTL (Time To Live) in key-value stores?

options.text: Automatic expiration—keys are deleted after a specified time

questions.explanation: TTL: set expiration time on keys. After TTL, key is automatically deleted. Perfect for: cache entries, session tokens, temporary data. Redis: EXPIRE, SETEX commands. Prevents stale data accumulation.

questions.question: A gaming app needs a real-time leaderboard showing top 100 players. Which is most suitable?
questions.explanation: Redis Sorted Sets: O(log n) insert/update, O(log n + m) range queries. ZADD to update scores, ZREVRANGE for top N. Perfect for leaderboards. MySQL would require expensive sorting on every query.
